content: The water authority has adopted a bottom-up strategy to address regulatory gaps by creating its own interim Drinking Water Regulatory Guidance and Compliance Standards. These standards encompass various aspects, including source water withdrawal and protection, treatment and distribution requirements, operator certification, and monitoring and reporting protocols, among other topics. Additionally, the water authority has successfully collaborated with Indigenous Services Canada, through the First Nations and Inuit Health Branch, to work with Nova Scotia Environment and Climate Change. This partnership aims to provide interim support until First Nations can establish their own regulatory framework. This includes conducting third-party reviews of the water authority’s adherence to the Drinking Water Regulatory Guidance and Compliance Standards, analyzing drinking water quality test results, and offering environmental public health guidance to address any adverse findings. While this collaboration is primarily advisory, it lays a critical foundation for future legally mandated regulatory activities. The Government of Canada acknowledges the importance of involving the Atlantic First Nations Water Authority and other service providers in shaping regulations and standards. In Ireland, approximately 11% of the population relies on private water supplies, which are exempt from national drinking water regulations. These recommendations are supported by resources aimed at raising awareness and providing technical assistance to private well owners. In South Africa, the Blue Drop certification program, introduced in 2008 by the Department of Water and Sanitation, incentivizes drinking water service providers to improve their performance. This program evaluates providers based on key performance areas such as capacity management, drinking water quality risk management, financial management, technical management, and compliance. Bonus points are awarded for process control training, performance agreements, public reporting of water quality results, and water demand management. Conversely, penalties are applied for data discrepancies or failure to report water quality failures. The program uses public performance reporting and benchmarking, as well as awards ceremonies, to encourage compliance and recognize excellence. These decrees are often complemented by cooperative agreements between water suppliers and farmers to prevent contamination from pesticides, pathogens, and nitrates. Farmers receive expert advice on sustainable practices, and in some cases, program costs are covered by abstraction fees. In the Philippines, the 2017 revision of the National Standards for Drinking Water introduced a risk-based approach to monitoring parameters. Parameters were categorized into mandatory, primary, and secondary groups based on health risks and local occurrence. Monitoring requirements were adjusted to reduce the burden on small water suppliers, with reduced frequency allowed if three years of data show undetectable contaminant levels. In the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, revised drinking water standards in 2014 set an interim arsenic limit of 50 µg/L for rural water supplies, recognizing their limited treatment capacity. This limit was reduced to 10 µg/L after five years. Iceland’s drinking water regulations require tiered monitoring frequencies based on the population served, with larger supplies undergoing more frequent testing. For example, systems serving fewer than 150 people require one test every two years, while those serving over 50,000 people require 34 tests annually, with additional tests for every 5,000 users. The European Union’s Drinking Water Directive allows for risk-based reductions in monitoring frequency or parameter lists, provided certain conditions are met, such as consistent low contaminant levels over three years and no anticipated factors that could degrade water quality. In Canada, field test kits are permitted for Escherichia coli testing in rural areas lacking access to accredited laboratories. These kits must be validated and used according to manufacturer instructions. Presence-absence testing is acceptable in some jurisdictions, as any positive detection of E. coli is sufficient for public health action. Nepal’s revised National Drinking Water Quality Standards allow the use of portable water test kits for microbial parameters, addressing challenges in data collection for small supplies. By 2023, these kits were in use in over 200 municipalities, contributing to improved data entry into the National Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene Management Information System. The regulatory authority has developed a standardized procedure for sampling and testing, ensuring consistency with laboratory results. This guidance is tailored to the skills of small water supply operators and aligns with ISO standards. Bhutan’s National Guideline for Drinking Water Quality Surveillance and Drinking Water Quality Standard outline reporting requirements for surveillance data. Immediate reporting is required for non-compliant results that pose public health risks. The government is undergoing water sector reforms, and these guidelines will be updated accordingly. In the Philippines, local government units are responsible for drinking water quality surveillance, including for small supplies. Guidelines issued in 2022 clarify roles and responsibilities and provide detailed instructions for forming local monitoring committees and conducting activities such as water safety plan audits and sanitary inspections. Surveillance findings must be reported monthly, quarterly, and annually, with public dissemination of water quality information. In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency’s Surface Water Treatment Rules require all public water supplies using surface water or groundwater under the influence of surface water to filter and disinfect their water unless specific criteria are met. These rules also establish treatment techniques to reduce microbial contaminants. Guidance manuals are available to assist small water supplies in meeting these requirements, detailing suitable disinfection and filtration technologies.
